title: Fruits of enterprize exhibited in the adventures of Belzoni in Egypt and Nubia : $b with an account of his discoveries in the pyramids, among the ruins of cities, and in the ancient tombs
summary: Fruits of enterprize exhibited in the adventures of Belzoni in Egypt and Nubia is a juvenile instructive travel narrative written in the early 19th century. Framed as conversations between a mother and her children, it recounts Giovanni Belzoni’s explorations in Egypt and Nubia—pyramids, temples, mummy caves, and his dramatic engineering to move the “Young Memnon” bust. Blending history, geography, and simple mechanics, it aims to entertain while sparking curiosity about ancient Egypt and the realities of travel and discovery. The opening of this work sets a warm family scene as a mother promises her curious children a true account of Egypt and of Belzoni, sketching the Nile’s geography, fertility, climate, and local customs. Belzoni arrives with a water-raising machine for irrigation, endures rough quarters, visits the pyramids at dawn, and amuses the viceroy Mahomed Ali with an electrical shock, but superstition and an accident doom his hydraulic project. He turns to antiquities, sails upriver with his wife, admires Dendera and the vast ruins of Thebes, and with levers, rollers, and a crude car begins hauling the colossal “Young Memnon” toward the Nile. A perilous crawl through a mummy cave reveals treacherous guides and the maze-like tombs; he then pushes on to Nubia—Elephantine, Philae, and Abu Simbel—where sand, time, and money halt his first attempt to open the great rock-cut temple. After a dangerous brush with the second cataract and a visit to the tiny island of Mainarty, he returns to Thebes and, by careful staging, succeeds in loading the bust onto a boat for Cairo and Rosetta. The next chapter opens with a lesson in perseverance at home and begins a second voyage up the Nile, reaching only as far as Minieh in the provided pages.
